title: COS_102 — End of Semester Objective Exam

questions.q: A flowchart reads: START, an input box "Input X", a process box "Y = 2 × X + 1", then a decision box "Is Y > 10?". The Yes branch goes to "Print Y − 10" and the No branch goes to "Print Y". Both branches reach STOP. The input is X = 4. What is printed?
questions.why:
The process box runs first: Y = 2 × 4 + 1 = 9. The test 9 > 10 is false, so the No branch runs and 9 is printed.

−1 takes the Yes branch and prints Y − 10; 8 drops the + 1 and computes only 2 × 4; 4 prints the input X instead of the value the process box produced.
questions.concept: Tracing a flowchart with a process and a decision

questions.q:
How many times does the loop body run?

```
n = 20
WHILE n > 3
    n = n − 4
ENDWHILE
```
questions.why:
n takes the values 20, 16, 12, 8, 4 at the top of each pass, and each of those is greater than 3, so the body runs 5 times. It leaves n at 0, and 0 > 3 is false, so the loop ends.

4 stops when n reaches 4 and forgets that 4 > 3 is still true; 6 counts the failing test as a pass of the body; 17 is 20 − 3 and counts single steps rather than steps of 4.
questions.concept: Counting iterations of a subtracting WHILE loop

questions.q: "Is there a delivery route from the depot to the market that costs less than ₦5,000?" Which type of computational problem is this?
questions.why:
The only thing asked for is YES or NO: either such a route exists or it does not. A problem whose solution is YES or NO is a decision problem.

A search problem would ask for the route itself; an optimization problem would ask for the cheapest route of all; a counting problem would ask how many routes cost less than ₦5,000.
questions.concept: Classifying a computational problem type

questions.q: A program reads two whole numbers and prints the first divided by the second. The compiler accepts it without complaint. It works on most runs, but when the user types 0 as the second number the program stops part way through with a division error. Which type of error is this?
options: Not an error, since most runs work
questions.why:
The program was built successfully and only fails while it is running, and only for one input. An error that appears during execution and stops the run is a run time error.

A syntax error would have stopped the compiler accepting the program at all; a logical error would let the run finish and give a wrong answer; a program that crashes on a legal input is faulty however many other runs succeed.
questions.concept: Classifying an error as syntax, logical or run time

questions.q: A plan reads: 1. Divide total by count and print the result. 2. Read count. 3. Read count numbers, adding each one to total. 4. Stop. Which required property of an algorithm's steps does this plan break?
questions.why:
Step 1 uses total and count before either of them has been read, so the steps are in the wrong order: the division happens on values that do not yet exist. The steps are not ordered.

Every step says exactly what to do, so unambiguous holds; nothing needed is missing, so complete holds; "none" ignores that the first step depends on results produced by the two steps after it.
questions.concept: Identifying which algorithm property a plan violates

questions.q:
What does this print?

```
n = 6
r = 1
WHILE n > 1
    r = r × n
    n = n − 2
ENDWHILE
PRINT r
```
questions.why:
Pass 1: r = 1 × 6 = 6, n = 4. Pass 2: r = 6 × 4 = 24, n = 2. Pass 3: r = 24 × 2 = 48, n = 0. Now 0 > 1 is false, so 48 is printed.

720 subtracts 1 from n instead of 2 and gives 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2; 24 stops one pass early at n = 2; 6 keeps only the first multiplication and forgets that r accumulates.
questions.concept: Tracing a WHILE loop that builds a product

questions.q: A program prints payslips. Which of these is a process the program carries out, rather than an input, an output or a device?
options: Multiplying hours worked by the hourly rate to get gross pay
The hours worked by each employee
The printer the payslips come out on
questions.why:
A process is work the program does on the data it was given. Multiplying hours by rate turns input data into a result, so it is a process.

The hours worked exist before the program runs and are given to it, so they are input; the printed payslip is what the program produces, so it is output; the printer is a device the output goes to, not part of the program at all.
questions.concept: Separating inputs, processes and outputs

questions.q: A program has been in use for two years. A new programmer joins the team and must change the way tax is worked out inside it. Which kind of documentation does that programmer need?
questions.why:
Programmer documentation carries the technical detail needed to upgrade and maintain a program, which is exactly what someone changing the tax calculation must have.

User documentation tells an end user how to install and use the program, not how it works inside; installation instructions are one part of that user documentation; a bug list records faults but does not explain the design.
questions.concept: User versus programmer documentation

questions.q: Which fragment prints the larger of two numbers A and B, and prints EQUAL when the two are the same?
options: IF A > B THEN PRINT A ELSE IF B > A THEN PRINT B ELSE PRINT "EQUAL"
IF A > B THEN PRINT A ELSE PRINT B
IF A > B THEN PRINT A; IF B > A THEN PRINT B; PRINT "EQUAL"
IF A ≥ B THEN PRINT A ELSE PRINT "EQUAL"
questions.why:
Three outcomes need three branches: A larger, B larger, and the two equal. Only the chain IF A > B ... ELSE IF B > A ... ELSE prints exactly one of the three, and prints EQUAL only when neither is larger.

The two-branch version prints B when the numbers are equal instead of EQUAL; the version with separate IFs prints EQUAL on every run, because that line is never guarded; the last one prints EQUAL whenever B is larger, which is wrong.
questions.concept: Choosing the correct implementation of a three-way test

questions.q: A machine has two switches, each with three positions, and one dial with four positions. An engineer finds the one working configuration by trial and error, testing each configuration once and never repeating one. How many tests does the worst case need?
questions.why:
Each configuration is one choice per control, so the count is 3 × 3 × 4 = 36. In the worst case the working one is tested last, so 36 tests are needed.

10 adds the positions, 3 + 3 + 4, instead of multiplying them; 12 uses only one switch and the dial, 3 × 4; 24 counts the pair of switches as a single factor of 2, giving 2 × 3 × 4.
questions.concept: Counting the trials a trial-and-error search needs

questions.q: A substitution puzzle allows the replacements AB → BBA and BB → A. Starting from AAB, apply AB → BBA once, then apply BB → A once to the word you get. Which word do you reach?
questions.why:
AAB contains AB in its last two letters, so AB → BBA turns it into ABBA. ABBA contains BB in the middle, so BB → A turns it into AAA.

ABBA is the word after only the first replacement; AA comes from deleting BB rather than replacing it with A; BBAA applies the first rule to the wrong place, treating the leading letters as the AB.
questions.concept: Applying substitution rules in order

questions.q: A university must place 900 students in hostel rooms so that students who apply together stay together. The goal and the constraints are stated exactly, but no standard procedure for doing it exists anywhere in the university. How is this problem classified?
questions.why:
The goal and the constraints are stated exactly, so the problem is well defined. No standard method exists, so a new method must be invented, which makes it non-routine.

Routine would mean the only work is picking a known algorithm, which is not the case here; the two ill-defined options are wrong because nothing about the goal or the constraints is left vague.
questions.concept: Routine versus non-routine and well versus ill defined

questions.q: A library must digitise 12,000 books in five months. In the first month only 800 can be done while staff are trained. Means-ends analysis splits the remainder into four equal monthly targets. What is each of those four targets?
questions.why:
After the first month 12,000 − 800 = 11,200 books remain, and four equal months share them: 11,200 / 4 = 2,800 books per month.

2,400 divides the whole 12,000 by 5 and ignores the reduced first month; 3,000 divides the whole 12,000 by 4 and forgets the 800 already done; 2,240 divides the correct remainder by 5 months instead of the 4 that are left.
questions.concept: Setting sub-goals with means-ends analysis

questions.q: A driver leaving a car park must reach the airport and has no map. Without pausing to weigh the options, she takes the road carrying the heaviest traffic, on the rule of thumb that at this hour most traffic is airport bound, and does not reconsider the choice. Which problem-solving strategy is this?
questions.why:
One shortcut is taken without stopping to think about the next course of action, and it is accepted without checking. That is a heuristic: fast, energy saving, and not guaranteed to be rational.

Trial and error would test one road, reject it and try another; means-ends analysis would fix the end and split the journey into sub-goals planned in advance; brainstorming needs a group producing many ideas.
questions.concept: Identifying the strategy from a described case

questions.q: In Alan Turing's universal machine, where is the program that describes the task to be carried out?
options: In the fixed table of instructions built into the machine
On the tape, written as a string of letters
In the read head that scans the tape
In a second machine built for that one task
questions.why:
The universal machine has one fixed instruction table and reads the particular task from its tape, where the program sits as a string of letters. That is the idea behind storing encoded instructions in a computer's memory.

The fixed table is the machine's own unchanging structure, not the task; the read head only scans; a separate machine per task is precisely what the universal machine removes the need for.
questions.concept: How the universal Turing machine holds a program

questions.q: Which of these questions has no algorithm that answers it correctly for every possible input?
options: Is this whole number divisible by 3?
Does this list of 500 names contain "Ada"?
Which of these 40 routes is the shortest?
Will this program eventually stop when it is run on this input?
questions.why:
Asking whether an arbitrary program halts on an arbitrary input is the halting problem, and no algorithm decides it correctly for every program and input.

Testing divisibility by 3 is a short calculation; scanning 500 names for a match is a straightforward search; comparing 40 route lengths is finite work, so all three of those have algorithms.
questions.concept: Recognising an undecidable question

questions.q: Solvable problems are grouped as data-structure based or algorithm based. Which of these is data-structure based?
options: Sorting a list of names into alphabetical order
Holding a queue of print jobs so the earliest is served first
Searching a sorted list by repeated halving
Splitting a task in two and combining the two results
questions.why:
The print jobs problem is solved by choosing the right way to store the items, a queue, so it belongs to the group based on data structures such as stacks, queues, arrays and trees.

Sorting, searching and divide and conquer are all named methods of doing work, so each of those is algorithm based rather than data-structure based.
questions.concept: Data-structure based versus algorithm based problems

questions.q: A password is exactly 3 characters long and every character is one of the 26 lowercase letters. A brute force attack tries the possible passwords one after another, and each attempt takes 0.002 seconds. How long does it take on average?
questions.why:
There are 26 × 26 × 26 = 17,576 passwords, so trying them all takes 17,576 × 0.002 = 35.152 seconds. On average the right one is found half way through, which is 35.152 / 2 = 17.576 seconds.

35.152 seconds is the worst case, not the average; 31.2 seconds uses 26 × 25 × 24 and wrongly forbids repeated letters; 0.156 seconds counts only 26 × 3 attempts, adding the positions instead of multiplying.
questions.concept: Average and worst case cost of a brute force search

questions.q: Coins of value 1, 6 and 10 are available in unlimited numbers. A greedy algorithm makes up an amount by repeatedly taking the largest coin that still fits. For the amount 12, how many coins does greedy use, and what is the smallest number of coins possible?
questions.why:
Greedy takes 10, leaving 2, which only the 1 coins can fill: 10 + 1 + 1, so 3 coins. But 6 + 6 makes 12 with 2 coins, so the greedy answer is not the best one.

Greedy cannot reach 2 coins here because its first choice of 10 is never revisited; the smallest is not 3, since 6 + 6 exists; greedy does not need 4 coins, as 10 + 1 + 1 already works.
questions.concept: Showing that a greedy choice need not be optimal

questions.q: Before a payroll program is released, a team writes a list of test scenarios with success criteria, feeds the program a negative number of hours worked, and checks that it rejects the entry instead of paying a negative wage. Which computational method is this?
questions.why:
Evaluating whether a program works as expected before it is released, by measuring it against a set of test scenarios and success criteria, is performance testing. Feeding it erroneous data is one of its standard forms.

Hypothesis testing evaluates a prediction using a null hypothesis, a significance level and a p-value; data mining extracts patterns from large data sets; backtracking retreats from rejected states while searching.
questions.concept: Identifying performance testing from a described case

questions.q: A trial is run at a significance level of 0.10 and the data give a p-value of 0.12. What is the decision, and what does it establish?
options: Reject the null hypothesis; the evidence against it is strong enough
Accept the null hypothesis; the null hypothesis is now proved true
Reject the null hypothesis; the significance level should be raised to 0.12
Accept the null hypothesis; the evidence against it was not strong enough
questions.why:
The rule is to reject the null hypothesis when the p-value is less than or equal to the significance level. Here 0.12 is greater than 0.10, so the null hypothesis is accepted, meaning only that the evidence against it was not strong enough.

The two reject options apply the rule backwards; accepting never proves the null hypothesis true; and the significance level is fixed in advance, not adjusted to match the p-value that came out.
questions.concept: Applying the p-value decision rule

questions.q: A staircase of n steps is climbed 1 or 2 steps at a time. The number of ways w(n) satisfies w(n) = w(n − 1) + w(n − 2), with w(1) = 1 and w(2) = 2, and each value is worked out once and stored in a table. What is w(6)?
questions.why:
Filling the table upwards: w(3) = 2 + 1 = 3, w(4) = 3 + 2 = 5, w(5) = 5 + 3 = 8, w(6) = 8 + 5 = 13.

8 is w(5) and stops one row early; 21 is w(7) and runs one row too far; 12 comes from starting the table at w(1) = 1 and w(2) = 1 instead of w(2) = 2.
questions.concept: Building a dynamic programming table from a recurrence

questions.q: A supermarket chain examines two years of till receipts, finds that customers who buy nappies on a Friday evening often buy beer in the same basket, and moves the two shelves closer together. Which computational method is this?
questions.why:
A large data set is searched for a pattern nobody had noticed, and the relationship found is used to make a decision. That is data mining.

Visualisation would draw the figures so a person could see them; pipelining would pass the output of one stage into the next; problem recognition would be about making sure the solution attacks the root cause.
questions.concept: Identifying data mining from a described case

questions.q: A study is designed so that there is at most a 1% chance of concluding that a new drug works when in fact it does not. Which significance level does that require?
questions.why:
The significance level is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true, which here is the chance of announcing an effect that does not exist. A 1% risk is a significance level of 0.01.

0.05 allows a 5% risk and 0.10 a 10% risk, both larger than the study permits; 0.99 would allow a 99% risk, which is the complement of a level, not a level.
questions.concept: Choosing a significance level from the risk allowed

questions.q: A routine finds the largest of 8 numbers by splitting the list into two halves, finding the largest in each half in the same way, and returning the larger of the two results. A list of one number is returned unchanged. How many comparisons of two numbers does the whole routine make?
questions.why:
Comparisons happen only when two results are combined. Eight numbers give 4 comparisons of pairs, then 2 comparisons of those 4 results, then 1 final comparison: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7.

8 counts one comparison per number and forgets that single numbers are returned without any comparison; 3 counts the levels of splitting rather than the comparisons; 4 counts only the first round of pairs.
questions.concept: Counting the combine steps in a divide and conquer routine

questions.q: Which of these does dynamic programming guarantee, where a greedy algorithm does not?
options: A shorter running time on every input
An optimal solution whenever a solution exists
Less memory use than any other method
That the first choice made is never changed later
questions.why:
Provided a solution to the problem exists, dynamic programming guarantees that an optimal one can be found, because sub-problem results are saved and compared rather than committed to. Greedy carries no such guarantee.

Dynamic programming is often slower and uses more memory than greedy, since it stores a table of results; never changing an early choice describes greedy, and is exactly why greedy can miss the optimum.
questions.concept: What dynamic programming guarantees

questions.q:
What is the time complexity of this fragment in terms of n?

```
i = 1
WHILE i ≤ n
    j = n
    WHILE j > 1
        j = j / 2
    ENDWHILE
    i = i + 1
ENDWHILE
```
questions.why:
The outer loop adds a constant to i, so it runs about n times, which is the O(n) rule. The inner loop divides j by a constant each pass, so it runs about log n times, which is the O(log n) rule. One inside the other gives O(n log n).

O(n²) would need the inner loop to step by a constant too; O(log n) counts only the inner loop; O(n) counts only the outer loop.
questions.concept: Big O of a loop nested inside a loop

questions.q: An algorithm solves a problem of size n by calling itself twice on problems of size n − 1 and doing a fixed amount of extra work. Which growth rate does it have?
questions.why:
Each call spawns two calls one size smaller, so the number of calls doubles at every level down to size 1, giving roughly 2ⁿ calls: O(2ⁿ).

O(n²) belongs to nested loops stepping by a constant; O(n log n) to a linear loop containing a halving loop; O(log log n) to a loop whose variable is changed exponentially each pass.
questions.concept: Big O of a doubly recursive algorithm

questions.q:
What does this print?

```
c = 0
FOR i = 1 TO 4
    FOR j = i TO 4
        c = c + 1
    ENDFOR
ENDFOR
PRINT c
```
questions.why:
The inner loop runs from i to 4, so it runs 4 times when i = 1, 3 times when i = 2, 2 times when i = 3 and once when i = 4: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10.

16 assumes the inner loop always runs 4 times, as if it started at 1; 12 uses 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 but drops the last pass and adds an extra outer round; 6 is 3 + 2 + 1 and forgets the pass where i = 1.
questions.concept: Counting executions of an inner loop with a moving bound

questions.q: A designer holds a finished algorithm and asks two questions about it: can it solve only this one problem or more general ones as well, and can its complexity be reduced? Which step of algorithm development is this?
questions.why:
Confirming that a finished algorithm solves the problem, asking whether it generalises and whether its complexity can be cut, is the review step, the last of the five.

Problem analysis fixes the starting and ending points before anything is written; high-level development produces the main outline; refinement adds detail to the outline, guided by who will implement it.
questions.concept: Identifying the algorithm development step

questions.q: A client's description states what the program must print when a mark is 50 or more, and what it must print when a mark is below 40, but says nothing at all about marks from 40 to 49. Which problem-description issue is this?
options: A description resting on unstated assumptions
questions.why:
A whole range of inputs has no stated behaviour, so a case is missing rather than unclear. That is an incomplete description.

An ambiguous description would state something that could be read two ways; an unstated assumption would be a rule the client took for granted but never said; posterior analysis is measurement of a finished program, not a description fault at all.
questions.concept: Naming the fault in a problem description

questions.q: A sorted list holds 1,000 items. A search repeatedly halves the range still to be examined, checking one item each time. At most how many items does it check?
questions.why:
Each check halves the range, so k checks cover up to 2^k items. 2⁹ = 512 is not enough for 1,000 but 2¹⁰ = 1,024 is, so at most 10 items are checked.

9 uses 2⁹ = 512 and does not cover 1,000; 500 counts one halving only; 1,000 is the worst case of checking every item one at a time, which is what halving avoids.
questions.concept: Worst case of a halving search

questions.q: A team runs a finished Java program on real data and records that it takes 3 seconds and uses 40 MB of memory. Which pair of terms describes what they did?
options: Priori analysis, measuring time and space complexity
Posterior analysis, measuring best and worst case
Priori analysis, measuring the growth rate
Posterior analysis, measuring time and space complexity
questions.why:
The work was done after the algorithm had been implemented in a particular language and run, which is posterior analysis, and the two quantities recorded are running time and space.

Priori analysis happens before implementation and is language independent; best and worst case describe how time varies with the input, not the two figures measured here; growth rate is what Big O describes, and it is not read off a single run.
questions.concept: Priori versus posterior analysis

questions.q: A program is built so that another designer can add new kinds of report to it later without rewriting what is already there. Which algorithm design factor is this?
questions.why:
Extensibility is the factor about another programmer or designer being able to update and upgrade the solution later, which is exactly what adding new report types means.

Modularity is breaking this solution into smaller steps; robustness is having the problem and its solution clearly defined so it holds up beyond the neat case; correctness is producing the right result.
questions.concept: Naming an algorithm design factor

questions.q: A flowchart runs: Start; "T = 0"; "K = 1"; decision "Is K ≤ 6?"; its No branch goes to "Print T" then Stop; its Yes branch goes to a second decision "Is K a multiple of 3?", whose Yes branch goes to "T = T + K" and whose No branch goes straight on; both then reach "K = K + 1", which flows back to the first decision. What is printed?
questions.why:
K runs from 1 to 6. Only K = 3 and K = 6 pass the multiple-of-3 test, so T = 3 then T = 3 + 6 = 9. When K becomes 7 the first test fails and 9 is printed.

21 adds every K and ignores the inner decision; 6 keeps only the last multiple of 3 and forgets that T accumulates; 3 leaves the loop at the first match.
questions.concept: Tracing a flowchart loop containing a decision

questions.q: A flowchart runs: Start; "Read A"; decision "Is A < 0?"; the Yes branch goes to "Print NEGATIVE" and the No branch to "Print A"; both arrows then meet at a merge, which flows to Stop. How many input/output symbols does the chart contain?
questions.why:
Input/output symbols are the parallelograms: Read A, Print NEGATIVE and Print A. That is 3.

2 counts only the two prints and forgets the read; 4 counts the decision diamond as well, but a diamond is a decision symbol; 1 counts only the read and treats printing as something other than output.
questions.concept: Counting flowchart symbols by type

questions.q: A flowchart has one Start and one Stop. One diamond, "Is x > 5?", has a single arrow entering it and a single arrow labelled Yes leaving it, with nothing drawn for the other outcome. Which rule does the chart break?
options: A decision must have exactly two exits, both labelled
A chart must have exactly one start terminator
Flow lines should not cross one another
Every chart must contain at least one loop
questions.why:
A decision symbol asks a yes/no question, so both answers must lead somewhere and both exits must be labelled. With only the Yes exit drawn, an input with x ≤ 5 has nowhere to go and the chart cannot be traced.

The chart already has exactly one start, so that rule is kept; no lines cross here; and loops are not required in a valid chart at all.
questions.concept: Spotting an invalid flowchart

questions.q: A chart sets Count to 0 and Total to 0 before its loop begins, and the person drawing it wants those steps drawn differently from the steps that do the actual work. Which symbol should they use for them?
options: A hexagon, pointed at both ends
A rectangle with a wavy bottom edge
questions.why:
The preparation symbol, a hexagon pointed at both ends, is the one that separates steps preparing for work, such as initialising a total or setting a counter, from steps that do the work.

A plain rectangle is the ordinary process symbol used for the working steps; a parallelogram is input or output; a wavy-bottomed rectangle means a document.
questions.concept: Choosing the flowchart symbol for a setting-up step

questions.q: A step in a chart must show that customer records are being kept in and fetched from permanent storage. Which symbol shows that?
options: A rectangle with a wavy bottom edge
A rectangle with a double line down each vertical side
questions.why:
The cylinder, drawn as a drum on its side, is the database symbol and shows where data is stored.

The wavy-bottomed rectangle is a document; the parallelogram is data moving in or out at that step rather than the store itself; the rectangle with double vertical lines is a predefined process, an operation defined elsewhere.
questions.concept: Matching a flowchart symbol to its purpose

questions.q: A flowchart runs: Start; "Read M"; decision "Is M ≥ 70?"; Yes goes to "Print A" then Stop; No goes to decision "Is M ≥ 50?"; Yes goes to "Print B" then Stop; No goes to "Print F" then Stop. The chart is run three times, with M = 70, then M = 69, then M = 50. What is printed on the three runs, in order?
questions.why:
M = 70 passes 70 ≥ 70 and prints A. M = 69 fails the first test but passes 69 ≥ 50 and prints B. M = 50 fails the first test and passes 50 ≥ 50, so it prints B too.

A, A, B reads the first test as M > 65 or similar and sends 69 to A; A, B, F reads the second test as M > 50, so 50 falls through to F; B, B, F reads the first test as M > 70, so 70 misses A.
questions.concept: Tracing nested decisions on boundary values

questions.q: One step in the middle of a large flowchart has to be changed. Why is that more troublesome than changing the same step written as pseudocode?
options: A flowchart cannot show a loop at all
The chart may have to be redrawn, and a complex chart can already run over several pages
A flowchart has to be compiled again after every change
A flowchart has no start or stop point to work from
questions.why:
Two of the stated disadvantages of flowcharts are that complex processes may span several pages and that adjustments are complicated and may require a redraw. Pseudocode is edited as text with no drawing at all.

Flowcharts do show loops, using a backward flow line from a decision; nothing in the three representations is ever compiled; and a valid chart always has a start and a stop point.
questions.concept: Advantages and disadvantages of flowcharts

questions.q: A designer wants to attach the remark "rate fixed by the finance office" beside the box that computes tax, without changing the flow of the chart. How is that drawn?
options: As a note in an open bracket joined by a dashed line, with no flow arrows
As a parallelogram joined to the tax box by a flow arrow
As a hexagon placed just before the tax box
As a merge triangle placed just after the tax box
questions.why:
A comment is drawn as an open square bracket attached by a dashed line. It sits off the flow path and takes no flow arrows, so it adds a remark without changing what the chart does.

A parallelogram on a flow arrow would make the remark an input or output step; a hexagon would make it a preparation step; a merge triangle would join paths that were never split.
questions.concept: The comment symbol and the flow path

questions.q:
What is printed?

```
SET n TO 12
SET c TO 0
REPEAT
    SET n TO n − 5
    INCREMENT c
UNTIL n < 0
PRINT n, c
```
questions.why:
Pass 1: n = 7, c = 1, and 7 < 0 is false. Pass 2: n = 2, c = 2, and 2 < 0 is false. Pass 3: n = −3, c = 3, and −3 < 0 is true, so the loop stops and −3 and 3 are printed.

2 and 2 stops as soon as n can no longer lose a full 5, treating UNTIL as n < 5; −3 and 4 counts the final test as another pass; 12 and 0 assumes the test is made before the first pass, which is what WHILE does, not REPEAT.
questions.concept: Tracing a REPEAT-UNTIL loop

questions.q: Which of these runs its body exactly 6 times?
questions.why:
FOR bounds are inclusive at both ends, so FOR i = a TO b runs b − a + 1 times. FOR i = 0 TO 5 runs 5 − 0 + 1 = 6 times.

FOR i = 1 TO 5 runs 5 times; FOR i = 0 TO 6 runs 7 times; FOR i = 6 TO 0 has its bounds the wrong way round, so the body never runs at all.
questions.concept: Counting the passes of a FOR loop

questions.q:
The user enters 69. What is printed?

```
READ g
CASE g DIV 10 OF
    9: PRINT "A"
    8: PRINT "B"
    7: PRINT "C"
    OTHERS: PRINT "D"
ENDCASE
```
questions.why:
g DIV 10 is integer division, so 69 DIV 10 = 6. No listed condition matches 6, so the OTHERS branch runs and D is printed.

C would need the expression to be 7, which would come from rounding 6.9 up instead of taking the whole part; B would need 8; "nothing at all" forgets that OTHERS is exactly the default for unmatched values.
questions.concept: Tracing a CASE construct with an OTHERS branch

questions.q:
The first value the user enters is −4. What is printed?

```
SET t TO 0
READ n
WHILE n > 0
    SET t TO t + n
    READ n
ENDWHILE
PRINT t
```
options: Nothing, since the loop never ends
questions.why:
WHILE tests its condition before the first pass. −4 > 0 is false at once, so the body never runs, t keeps its initial value and 0 is printed.

−4 assumes the body runs once and adds n, which is what a REPEAT-UNTIL loop would do; the loop does end, immediately; 4 takes the size of the input and ignores its sign.
questions.concept: A WHILE body that runs zero times

questions.q:
This is meant to print the largest of the four values entered, but for the inputs −7, −2, −9 and −5 it prints 0.

```
SET big TO 0
FOR i = 1 TO 4
    READ x
    IF x > big THEN
        SET big TO x
    ENDIF
ENDFOR
PRINT big
```

Which change makes it correct for any four values?
options: Change IF x > big to IF x < big
Read the first value before the loop, set big to it, and loop over the other three
Move SET big TO 0 inside the loop, before READ x
Change FOR i = 1 TO 4 to FOR i = 0 TO 4
questions.why:
big starts at 0, and no negative input is ever greater than 0, so nothing replaces it. Seeding big with the first value actually entered removes the assumption that some input beats 0, and the remaining three are then compared against it. For −7, −2, −9, −5 the fixed version prints −2.

Reversing the test makes it find the smallest; resetting big inside the loop throws away the running best every pass; extending the loop bound reads a fifth value that does not exist and still starts from 0.
questions.concept: Fixing a maximum search with a bad starting value

questions.q:
Which line breaks a rule of pseudocode, and which rule does it break?

```
1  SET total TO 0
2  FOR i = 1 TO 3
3      READ mark
4      System.out.println(mark)
5      SET total TO total + mark
6  ENDFOR
7  PRINT total
```
options: Line 2; keywords must be written in capital letters
Line 5; only one statement is allowed on a line
Line 6; a FOR construct is closed with ENDWHILE
Line 4; statements must be language independent
questions.why:
Line 4 is a Java statement. Pseudocode statements must be language independent, so that anyone can read them and they can be converted into any language; DISPLAY mark or PRINT mark is what belongs there.

Line 2 already has FOR in capitals; line 5 holds one statement, not several; and ENDFOR on line 6 is the correct closing keyword for FOR, so nothing is wrong there.
questions.concept: Applying the rules that govern pseudocode

questions.q: A loop ends with `UNTIL x > 100`. Which WHILE loop repeats the same body on the same values?
options: WHILE x ≤ 100, with one copy of the body also placed before the loop
questions.why:
REPEAT continues while its UNTIL condition is false, so UNTIL x > 100 corresponds to WHILE x ≤ 100. REPEAT also always runs its body once before testing, so the body has to appear once before the WHILE as well, otherwise a first value above 100 skips it entirely.

WHILE x > 100 keeps the condition instead of inverting it and runs exactly when the REPEAT would stop; WHILE x ≥ 100 inverts it wrongly and misses x = 100; WHILE x ≠ 100 loops on every value except 100.
questions.concept: Converting REPEAT-UNTIL into WHILE

questions.q: A routine named Discount takes a price and hands back the reduced price. Which line calls it so that the reduced price ends up in newPrice?
options: CALL Discount with price RETURNING newPrice
CALL Discount with newPrice RETURNING price
CALL Discount RETURNING price with newPrice
CALL newPrice with price RETURNING Discount
questions.why:
In a CALL line, `with` names what is passed in and `RETURNING` names the variable that receives what comes back. The price goes in and the reduced price comes back into newPrice.

The second option passes the empty result in and writes the answer back over the original price; the third returns into price and passes newPrice in, the same swap in a different order; the fourth treats the routine's own name as the variable being filled.
questions.concept: Reading a CALL with arguments and a return value

questions.q:
Every value here is an int. What is the value of the expression?

```c
40 - 12 / 3 * 2
```
questions.why:
`/` and `*` sit at the same precedence level and associate left to right, so 12 / 3 = 4 first, then 4 * 2 = 8, and finally 40 - 8 = 32.

18 works straight left to right, (40 - 12) / 3 * 2; 38 treats `*` as outranking `/`, giving 12 / (3 * 2) = 2; 72 does the subtraction before the multiplication, (40 - 4) * 2.
questions.concept: Operator precedence and associativity in C

questions.why:
The operand types choose the operation, and the variable it is stored in has no say. In x both operands are int, so 9 / 4 is integer division giving 2, widened to 2.00. In y the cast makes the left operand a float before the division, so the division is a real one and gives 2.25. In z the division has already been done in int, so the cast only widens 2 to 2.00.

2.25 for x assumes a float target forces real division; 2.25 for z casts after the damage is done; 2.00 for y misses that the cast is applied before the division.
questions.concept: Integer division and where the cast goes

questions.q: `int a = 45, b = 26;` What are the values of `a & b`, `a | b` and `a ^ b`, in that order?
questions.why:
45 is 101101 and 26 is 011010. AND keeps a bit only where both have it: 001000 = 8. OR keeps a bit where either has it: 111111 = 63. XOR keeps a bit where exactly one has it: 110111 = 55.

63, 8, 55 swaps the roles of `&` and `|`; 8, 71, 55 adds the two numbers instead of ORing them, since 45 + 26 = 71; 8, 55, 63 swaps `|` and `^`.
questions.concept: Bitwise AND, OR and XOR on two integers

questions.why:
`i++` yields the value before the increment, 0, so 0 > 0 is false and i becomes 1. Because the left operand of `&&` is false the whole expression is already 0, so the right operand is never evaluated and `j++` never runs. That gives r = 0, i = 1, j = 0.

0 1 1 evaluates both operands, which is what `&` would do; 1 1 1 reads `i++` as `++i`, so that 1 > 0 is true; 0 0 0 forgets that `i++` still increments i even though it yields 0.
questions.concept: Short-circuit evaluation and side effects

questions.why:
Each compound assignment is the plain operation applied to x: 20 - 6 = 14, then 14 * 2 = 28, then 28 % 9 = 1, then 1 + 5 = 6.

12 does the multiplication before the subtraction, 20 * 2 - 6 = 34, then 34 % 9 = 7 and 7 + 5 = 12; 14 reads `x %= 9` backwards as x = 9 % x, giving 9 % 28 = 9 and then 14; 8 reads `%=` as division, taking 28 / 9 = 3 and then 3 + 5 = 8.
questions.concept: Tracing compound assignment operators

questions.q: A record must hold a product name of up to 24 characters, a price as a double and a stock count as an int, and all three must be readable at the same time. Taking char as 1 byte, int as 4 bytes, double as 8 bytes and no padding, which construct is needed and how many bytes does one record occupy?
questions.why:
All three values must exist at once, so every member needs its own storage. That is a structure, and its size is the sum of its members: 24 + 8 + 4 = 36 bytes.

A union gives every member the same starting address, so it can represent only one member at a time and its size is that of the largest member, 24 bytes, which is why both union answers are wrong here. A union of 36 bytes adds members that share storage; a structure of 24 bytes applies the union size rule to a structure.
questions.concept: Choosing between a structure and a union

questions.q: Every occurrence of the variable `n` in a working C program is renamed `itemCount`, and nothing else is changed. What happens when the program is recompiled and run?
options: It behaves exactly as before, because names are replaced by memory addresses
It runs more slowly, because a longer name takes more memory at run time
It fails, because the address bound to n is lost
Its stored values change, because the name is kept in memory beside the value
questions.why:
Variable names are not stored inside memory while the program runs. The compiler replaces each name with the address of the location it stands for, so a consistent rename produces the same addresses and the same instructions and the program behaves identically.

Name length costs nothing at run time, so no slowdown; nothing is bound to a name at run time for the rename to lose; and the bytes at an address hold the value only, never the name.
questions.concept: Variable names versus memory addresses

questions.why:
A char holds a character's numeric code, so `c - 'A'` is 68 - 65 = 3. `c + 1` is 69, which `%c` prints as the character E. `'Z' - c` is 90 - 68 = 22.

4 E 23 counts the letters inclusively instead of subtracting the codes; 68 E 22 prints the code of 'D' itself rather than the difference; 3 E 21 is one short at the end, as if 'Z' were 89.
questions.concept: Character codes and arithmetic on char

questions.why:
f(4) = 16 - 1 = 15 and f(3) = 9 - 1 = 8, so g(4) = 15 + 8 = 23.

30 calls f(4) twice instead of f(4) and f(3); 15 keeps only the first term; 24 forgets the -1 in the second call, adding 15 + 9.
questions.concept: Evaluating a function that calls another function

questions.why:
`return` supplies a value and ends the function immediately, loop and all. i = 1 and i = 2 each add one, so c = 2; at i = 3 the test 3 % 3 == 0 is true and 2 is returned there and then.

5 treats `return` as skipping only that one pass, counting 1, 2, 4, 5, 7; 7 ignores the return and counts every value; 3 returns i rather than c.
questions.concept: return ends a function immediately

questions.why:
The parameter n is a local copy, and inside twice it shadows the global n. Doubling the copy gives the returned value 10, while the global n was never assigned to and is still 5.

10 10 treats the parameter and the global as one variable; 5 5 assumes a call cannot change anything at all, including its own result; 20 5 doubles once inside the function and again on the way out.
questions.concept: Parameters are local copies that shadow globals

questions.why:
`show` is declared `void`, which means it returns no value at all, so its call has nothing that can be stored and cannot appear on the right of an `=`.

The other three are legal: `grow` returns a double, so it can be stored in b or handed to `show`, and a void call is a perfectly good statement on its own. Note that `show` does print a number, but printing is not returning.
questions.concept: void functions have no value to assign

questions.q:
How many characters appear on the screen when this line runs?

```c
printf("a\\b\"c");
```
questions.why:
Inside a string literal a backslash always begins an escape. `\\` stands for one backslash and `\"` stands for one double quote, so the characters printed are a, backslash, b, double quote, c: five in all.

7 counts every escape as the two characters typed; 3 counts only the letters, treating the escapes as invisible; 4 reads the `\"` as ending the string, losing the quote and the c.
questions.concept: Escape sequences in a string literal

questions.q: A class keeps `balance` private and offers a public `deposit(amount)`. The body of `deposit` is later rewritten to record every deposit in a log before adding it, while its name, its one input and its return type stay the same. What happens to the programs that call `deposit`?
options: They break, because a public method's body is part of what callers depend on
They must have the new body copied into them before they will compile
They keep working, because they used only the name and the input and output formats
They can now reach balance directly, since deposit was changed
questions.why:
Functional abstraction means the implementation of a method is not exposed: all a caller needs is the method's name, the format of the input and the format of the output. Changing the body while leaving those three the same cannot break a caller, which is exactly why the implementation of a method can be changed without breaking other parts of the code.

The body was never something callers could depend on, so it neither breaks them nor has to be copied into them; and rewriting a method does nothing to the access specifier on the data, so balance stays private.
questions.concept: Functional abstraction and changing an implementation

questions.why:
vat(200) = 15.00 and vat(400) = 30.00, so gross returns 215.00 and 430.00 and their sum is 645.00.

600.00 forgets to add the VAT at all; 45.00 adds only the two VAT amounts; 615.00 adds the VAT of the first price only.
questions.concept: Tracing a function that calls another function

questions.why:
fee(1) meets the guard days <= 1 and returns 0. fee(4) returns 50 * (4 - 1) = 150. total is 0 + 150 = 150.

200 charges every day, 50 * 4; 250 charges 50 * (1 + 4), ignoring the free first day of each stay; 100 subtracts a day twice over, 50 * (4 - 2).
questions.concept: Tracing a guarded function called twice

questions.why:
The inner loop starts at j = i, so it runs 3 times when i = 1, twice when i = 2 and once when i = 3. The body runs 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 times.

9 assumes the inner loop always makes three passes; 3 counts the outer loop only; 12 counts four inner passes each time, as `j <= 3` from j = 0 would give.
questions.concept: Counting passes of a nested loop

questions.why:
First pass: 27 % 10 = 7 so s = 7, and 27 / 10 = 2 so n = 2. Second pass: n > 0 and s < 10 both hold, 2 % 10 = 2 so s = 9, and 2 / 10 = 0 so n = 0. The test n > 0 now fails, and 0 9 is printed.

2 7 stops after one pass; 9 0 prints the two values the wrong way round; 2 27 adds n itself instead of its last digit, so s reaches 27 and the s < 10 guard ends the loop early.
questions.concept: Tracing a while loop with a compound condition

questions.why:
An if-else-if chain stops at the first true condition and skips every later one. For m = 85 the first test 85 >= 50 is already true, so pass is printed and the distinction branch is never reached.

45 falls through both tests to the final else and correctly prints fail; 50 and 69 are passes and are printed as passes. Every mark of 70 or more is misclassified, and 85 is the only such mark offered.
questions.concept: Branch order in an if-else-if chain

questions.q: Which expression has the same value as `!(a >= 5 || b < 2)` for every a and b?
questions.why:
De Morgan's law turns the negation of an OR into the AND of the two negations: !(P || Q) is !P && !Q. The negation of a >= 5 is a < 5, and the negation of b < 2 is b >= 2, so the equivalent expression is a < 5 && b >= 2.

`a < 5 || b >= 2` negates both operands but forgets that the operator flips too; `a > 5 && b <= 2` merely reverses the two signs instead of negating them; `a <= 5 && b > 2` puts both boundary values on the wrong side, and disagrees at a = 5 or b = 2.
questions.concept: De Morgan's laws on a compound condition

questions.why:
A do-while tests after the body, so the body is guaranteed to run at least once whatever the condition says. That one pass makes c = 1 and i = 5, and the test 5 > 7 is then false, so the loop ends.

0 7 is what a while loop with the same condition would give, since 7 > 7 is false before the first pass; 1 7 runs the body but forgets that it changed i; 3 1 keeps looping while i is merely positive.
questions.concept: do-while runs its body at least once

questions.why:
Without braces a for statement governs exactly one statement, and indentation is invisible to the compiler, so only `s = s + i;` is repeated. The loop makes s = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 and leaves i = 5, then each printf runs once, giving 10 5.

1 3 6 10 5 treats the indented printf as part of the loop body; 10 4 forgets that i is incremented once more before the failing test; 15 5 adds the final i = 5 into the total as well.
questions.concept: Indentation does not make a block

questions.q: A statement moves program control to another line without testing anything at all. Which kind of branching is that, and which statement performs it?
questions.why:
Branching is any move of control away from the next line. When the move happens with no condition checked at all it is unconditional branching, and goto is the statement that does it.

if, if-else, if-else-if and switch move control only when a predetermined condition is satisfied, so all four are conditional branching, also called decision making or selection. That rules out if-else as unconditional and goto as conditional.
questions.concept: Unconditional versus conditional branching

questions.why:
Each pass raises i by 3 in total: 2 in the body and 1 in the increment step. At the top of the loop i is 0, 3, 6 and 9, so the body runs four times; after the fourth pass i is 12 and the test 12 < 12 fails.

12 12 ignores the `i = i + 2` inside the body; 4 11 forgets the increment step that runs after the last pass; 3 12 stops counting before the pass that starts at i = 9.
questions.concept: Tracing a for loop whose counter changes in the body

questions.q: Curly brackets are put around three statements inside a function. How does the computer then treat that group, and what follows the closing bracket?
options: As three separate statements, and a semicolon follows the closing bracket
As a single statement, and a semicolon follows the closing bracket
As a single statement, and no semicolon follows the closing bracket
As a nameless function, and no semicolon follows the closing bracket
questions.why:
A block is more than one statement inside curly brackets, and the group of statements inside it is treated like a single statement by the computer. That is precisely what lets a block stand wherever one statement is expected, which is why if, while and for each govern either one statement or one block. The right curly bracket does not have a semicolon after it.

Treating the group as three separate statements is what happens when the brackets are left off; and a block is not a function, so nothing is called and nothing is returned.
questions.concept: A block is treated as one statement

questions.why:
The index takes the values 1, 3, 5 and 7, so the elements added are a[1] = 1, a[3] = 3, a[5] = 2 and a[7] = 5, giving 11.

26 starts at i = 0 and adds 4 + 7 + 9 + 6; 37 adds all eight elements; 6 stops one step early, after i = 5.
questions.concept: Traversing an array with a stride

questions.why:
a takes its size from its initialiser, so it holds 4 elements and a[3], the element at offset 3, is 8. b is declared with 6 elements but given only 2 values, and too few initialisers is legal: the rest become 0. So b[2] and b[5] are both 0 and the line prints 8 0.

13 0 assumes b[2] is 5; 6 0 reads a[3] as the third value, forgetting that indexing is an offset from the first element; 8 5 assumes the last initialiser is repeated to fill the remaining slots.
questions.concept: Array initialisation and the zero-base index

questions.why:
The first subscript selects the row and the second selects the column, so m[i][1] walks down column 1 and picks up 5, 1 and 8, which total 14.

13 sums column 0, 2 + 7 + 4; 27 sums every element of the array; 8 keeps only the last value read instead of accumulating.
questions.concept: Reading one column of a two-dimensional array

questions.why:
The argument drops by 2 each call, so the calls are t(7), t(5), t(3), t(1), t(-1). The last meets the base case n <= 0 and returns 0, and the pending additions give 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 16.

28 steps down by 1 instead of 2, adding 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1; 15 drops the final 1, as a base case of n <= 1 would; 12 adds only the first two terms.
questions.concept: Tracing a recursive function with a step of two

questions.why:
The printf before the recursive call runs on the way down, printing 3, then 2, then 1. Control returns to the point just after each call, so the second printf runs on the way back up, in the reverse order, printing 1, then 2, then 3. The output is 321123.

321 assumes nothing written after a recursive call ever runs; 123321 puts the two printf lines the other way round; 333222 assumes each frame prints its own n twice before recursing.
questions.concept: Code after a recursive call runs on the way back up

questions.why:
Integer division halves the argument and throws away any fraction: 48, 24, 12, 6, 3, then 3 / 2 = 1. Five calls each add 1 before the base case n == 1 returns 0, so the result is 5.

6 counts the base case as a step as well, or treats 3 / 2 as 2 and inserts an extra halving; 4 stops at 3, assuming halving cannot reach 1 from there; 48 returns the argument instead of the number of halvings.
questions.concept: Tracing a recursive halving function

questions.why:
The recursive call already returns the largest of the first n - 1 elements, so the only work left is to compare it with the one element not yet considered. With n elements that element sits at offset n - 1, and returning the larger of the two gives the largest of all n. For {4, 9, 2} it returns 9.

`a[n]` reads one place past the last element, which is out of range and not diagnosed; returning m alone never examines the last element, so maxA({4, 9, 2}, 3) would give 9 but maxA({4, 2, 9}, 3) would give 4; adding them returns a total, not a maximum.
questions.concept: Completing the recursive case of a maximum

questions.q: A program declares `double t[6];`, fills all six elements, and then needs somewhere to put a seventh reading. Which is true?
options: Writing t[6] extends the array to seven elements
The compiler rejects any line that writes to t[6]
The size was fixed at the declaration, so there is no seventh element
The array grows by itself, since every element has the same type
questions.why:
An array stores a fixed-size sequential collection of elements of the same type, and the size is settled at the declaration and never changes while the program runs. The legal indices are t[0] to t[5].

t[6] is not a new slot: it names the memory just past the end of the block, so writing there quietly overwrites whatever else lives at that address. Nothing in C stores or checks a length at run time, so the compiler does not reject it and no error is reported; the program may finish and print a confident wrong answer.
questions.concept: Arrays are fixed-size and bounds are not checked

questions.why:
The first pass swaps a[0] with a[4] and the second swaps a[1] with a[3], so the array ends as 15, 12, 9, 6, 3. The middle element a[2] is never touched, and the line prints 15 9 3.

3 9 15 is the array left unchanged; 15 6 3 reads a[1] before its swap; 15 12 3 reads a[1] after its swap instead of a[2].
questions.concept: Tracing an in-place array swap

questions.q: A 5,000-line program is divided into twelve modules. Which of these effects is a disadvantage of dividing it?
options: Compilation and loading time may be longer
Smaller units are faster to design, develop and test
A small module is easier to understand
Modules can be reused in another program
questions.why:
The costs of modularisation are that execution time may be longer, storage size may be increased, compilation and loading time may be longer, inter-module communication problems may be increased, and more initial design time is demanded. Longer compilation and loading is one of those five.

The other three options are advantages: smaller units are easier and faster to design, develop, test and publish; a small module is easier to understand; and modules can be reused elsewhere in the program or in another program.
questions.concept: Advantages versus disadvantages of modularisation

questions.q: In a hierarchical design the top module decides which of three reports to produce and does no arithmetic, while the three modules below it read the file, compute the totals and print the report. Which partitioning is this, and what does the top module own?
options: Horizontal, the decision-making with little processing
Vertical, all the input, computation and output
Horizontal, communication between the functions and executing them
Vertical, the decision-making with little processing
questions.why:
In vertical partitioning functionality is distributed top-down: control modules at the top do the decision-making and little processing, while worker modules at the bottom perform all the input, computation and output. That is exactly the arrangement described.

Horizontal partitioning is the other one, where control modules communicate between the functions and execute them, so both horizontal answers name the wrong partition. Giving the top module all the input, computation and output describes the worker modules at the bottom instead.
questions.concept: Horizontal versus vertical structural partitioning

questions.q:
A module holds four functions.

```
module Payroll:
    compute_gross, compute_tax, compute_net, resize_logo
```

Which function should be moved out to another module, and which measure of module independence does moving it improve?
questions.why:
Cohesion is the extent to which the functions in a module work together to achieve the module's aim, and we want it high. Three of these functions serve the single aim of working out pay; resize_logo serves a different aim entirely, so it drags the module's cohesion down and belongs in a module of its own.

Moving compute_tax or compute_net would remove a function that does serve the module's aim, lowering cohesion further. Coupling is measured between modules, not inside one, so it is not the measure that this change improves.
questions.concept: Raising cohesion by moving an unrelated function

questions.q: A hierarchical design is partitioned horizontally, so that control modules communicate between the functions and execute them. What is the stated cost of that arrangement?
options: Worker modules can no longer perform input or output
More data must be passed across the module interface, making control flow more complex
Negative impacts spread through the design more quickly
The software becomes harder to extend with new functions
questions.why:
Horizontal partitioning requires passing more data across the module interface, which makes control flow more complex, especially where data moves rapidly from one function to another. That is the price paid for it.

Easier testing and maintenance, slowly spreading negative impacts and easy extension are the benefits of structural partitioning, so two of these options state the opposite of what partitioning buys. Worker modules doing all the input, computation and output belongs to vertical partitioning and is not something horizontal partitioning forbids.
questions.concept: The cost of horizontal partitioning

questions.q:
Coupling is counted as the number of other modules a module must call before it can do its work.

```
module Accounts: calls nothing outside itself
module Ledger:   calls Accounts.balance()
module Tax:      calls Accounts.balance()
module Invoice:  calls Ledger.post(), Accounts.balance(), Tax.rate()
```

Which module has the highest coupling and which has the lowest?
questions.why:
Count the other modules each one depends on: Accounts 0, Ledger 1, Tax 1, Invoice 3. Invoice has the highest coupling and Accounts the lowest, and low coupling is what we want, so Accounts is in the healthiest position.

Accounts highest counts how many modules call Accounts, which measures the opposite direction; Tax is not the lowest because Accounts depends on nothing at all; Ledger depends on one module only, so it cannot be the highest.
questions.concept: Measuring coupling between modules

questions.q: Module Stock stops exposing its internal table and offers only a `units(sku)` function, and the three modules that read the table are changed to call it. Stock later replaces the table with a different data structure. What does that replacement now cost?
options: Nothing outside Stock, since no other module can reach its data structures
Edits in all three modules, since each still depends on how Stock stores its data
Edits in the two modules that call units(sku) most often
Nothing anywhere, since changing a data structure is never a change at all
questions.why:
Information hiding means one module's data structures and processing details are not accessible to other modules, which are passed only as much information as they need. Once the three modules go through units(sku) they depend on that function, not on the table behind it, so replacing the table changes nothing outside Stock. That is the stated benefit: it restricts the effects of changes in one component on others.

The three modules no longer depend on the storage, so none of them needs editing, and how often a module calls the function has nothing to do with it. Stock itself certainly changes, so it is not true that nothing changes anywhere.
questions.concept: Information hiding restricts the effect of a change

questions.q: Design R has five modules, each doing one job and each calling only its own functions. Design S has five modules, each doing one job but each needing three of the others before it can run. Which measure separates the two designs, and which design is better on it?
options: Cohesion, and R is better because its cohesion is higher
Coupling, and S is better because its coupling is higher
Coupling, and R is better because its coupling is lower
Cohesion, and S is better because its cohesion is lower
questions.why:
Cohesion is judged inside a module, and both designs have modules that each do one job, so cohesion is high in both and cannot tell them apart. What differs is how far each module depends on other modules before it can perform its function, which is coupling, judged between modules. R depends on nothing and S on three others each, and low coupling is the goal, so R is better.

The two cohesion answers pick the measure that is the same in both designs, and high coupling or low cohesion is never the thing to aim for.
questions.concept: Cohesion inside a module, coupling between modules

questions.q: In one of the two generic design approaches the amount of abstraction increases with each higher level. Which approach is it, and where does it start?
options: Top-down, starting from the whole system as one entity
Bottom-up, starting from the most specific and basic components
Bottom-up, starting from the whole system as one entity
Top-down, starting from the most specific and basic components
questions.why:
Bottom-up design starts with the most specific and basic components and composes higher-level components from lower-level ones until the system evolves as one single component, and with each higher level the amount of abstraction is increased. It suits a system built from an existing set of primitives that can be reused.

Top-down works the other way: it takes the whole system as one entity and decomposes it into sub-systems, treating each as a system and decomposing again until the lowest level is reached, and it suits a design made from scratch when the specific details are unknown. That rules out both top-down answers, and bottom-up cannot start from the whole system.
questions.concept: Top-down versus bottom-up design

questions.q: A quantity field is specified as valid from 5 to 50 inclusive. Which set is exactly the six values that boundary value analysis tests for that range?
questions.why:
Defects cluster at the edges of a partition, so boundary value analysis takes the value just below, at, and just above each edge. The lower edge 5 gives 4, 5, 6 and the upper edge 50 gives 49, 50, 51.

5, 6, 7, 48, 49, 50 never leaves the valid range, so it cannot catch an implementation written as qty < 50; 0, 4, 5, 50, 51, 99 mixes in two values that are nowhere near an edge and drops 6 and 49; 4, 5, 49, 50, 51, 52 drops 6 and takes 52, which is two past the upper edge rather than one.
questions.concept: Boundary value analysis

questions.q: One unchanged build of an app is run on Chrome, Safari, Windows and Android, and the results are compared. Which method is this, and which of the two families does it belong to?
questions.why:
Compatibility testing determines whether the software works with different browsers, platforms and operating systems, that is every environment the end users will use. It is one of the four non-functional methods, alongside usability, performance and security.

System testing keeps the environment fixed and checks the integrated whole against the technical and functional requirements; acceptance testing confirms the software meets the expected requirements and is functional. Calling compatibility testing functional puts it in the family that asks whether the program does the right thing rather than how well it does it.
questions.concept: Classifying a non-functional testing method

questions.q: A tester is given the source of one function and chooses inputs so that each branch of its two if statements is executed at least once. Name the visibility class and the functional level.
questions.why:
The internal structure is known and the inputs were chosen to exercise paths through the code, which is white box testing. The target is a single function and its execution paths, which is unit testing.

Black box means the internals are not known to the tester; grey box uses partial internal knowledge only to design the cases, which are then run through the exposed interfaces; and acceptance testing is one of the levels black box applies to, not white box.
questions.concept: White box testing at the unit level

options: 9, and the last element is never examined
9, and m is reset on every pass
questions.why:
len(v) - 1 is 3, so i takes the values 0, 1 and 2 and the elements compared are 3, 9 and 2. m ends at 9 and the last element, 12, is never looked at. The fix is to loop over range(len(v)).

12 assumes the loop reaches the end; 3 ignores the update that does happen at i = 1; and m is set once before the loop, not on every pass, which is a different defect that would return 12 here only by accident.
questions.concept: Finding an off-by-one defect from a wrong result

questions.q: During which phase of the software testing life cycle are the software and hardware requirements for the test specified?
questions.why:
Test environment setup is the phase in which the software and hardware requirements for the test are specified, and its activities are test data setup and environment setup.

Test planning defines the testing strategy, cost and duration and identifies the testing environment without specifying its requirements; requirement analysis decides what is to be tested; test case development identifies, writes and reviews the test cases. Environment setup is the phase most often left out of the list of six.
questions.concept: Matching an activity to its STLC phase

questions.q: A test case reads: Inputs, an order of three items at 2,500 each. Expected output, a total of 7,500. Which of the three required parts of a test case is missing?
options: The process, that is what is done with the inputs
None, since all three parts are present
questions.why:
A test case gives detailed step-by-step instructions on how a test should be performed, specifying the test inputs, the process and the expected outputs. The inputs and the expected output are both given here, but nothing says what is to be done with them, so the tester does not know which function or screen to exercise.

The inputs are stated as three items at 2,500 each and the expected output as 7,500, so neither of those is missing, and a case with only two of the three parts is not complete.
questions.concept: The three parts of a test case

questions.q: A payment page returns the correct receipt every time, but each page takes 45 seconds to appear. Which is true of it?
options: It fails a functional test, because a result that slow is not the expected output
It passes a functional test and fails a non-functional one
It passes both, because the output produced is correct
It fails both, because a delay that long makes every result unusable
questions.why:
Functional testing asks whether the program performs as expected, that is whether the output it gives is the same as the expected output. The receipt is correct every time, so the functional test passes. Non-functional testing asks how well the software behaves, and response time under load is performance testing, which this page fails.

A correct answer delivered slowly is not a wrong answer, so the functional test cannot fail; and a passing functional test does not excuse the performance one.
questions.concept: Functional versus non-functional testing

questions.q: After every part is integrated, one run confirms that the whole product meets its technical and functional requirements. A later run by the customer's own staff confirms it meets their expected requirements and hunts for spelling mistakes and for bugs that cause crashes. Name the two methods in that order.
questions.why:
System testing tests the system as a whole after all the parts are integrated and confirms that it meets the technical and functional requirements. Acceptance testing confirms the software meets the expected requirements and, beyond issues such as spelling errors, identifies bugs that can cause major errors and software crashes.

Integration testing checks how well different parts work together and happens before the whole is assembled, so it cannot be the first run described; usability testing finds issues with the help of users who are observed while using the software, which is not what the second run does.
questions.concept: System testing versus acceptance testing
